sections.heading: Cosmos Hub and IBC
paragraphs: Per the file, the IBC protocol, famously implemented by the (per the file) Cosmos SDK, occupies a (per the file) similar problem space as (per the file) Wormhole - cross-chain message passing. Per the file, it is orthogonal to (per the file) Wormhole and solves a (per the file) larger and differently shaped (per the file) problem, leading to a different design. Per the file, iBC specifies a cross-chain (per the file) communication protocol with high-level semantics (per the file) like channels, ports, acknowledgments, ordering and timeouts.

Per the file, it is a stream (per the file) abstraction on top of (per the file) a packet/datagram transport, vaguely (per the file) similar to the TCP/IP protocol. Per the file, iBC is part of (per the file) the Cosmos Internet of (per the file) Blockchain scalability vision, with (per the file) hundreds or even thousands (per the file) of sovereign IBC-compatible chains (per the file) (called "zones") communicating via IBC (per the file) using a hub-and-spoke topology. Per the file, data availability is provided by permissionless relayers.

Per the file, with IBC, for two (per the file) chains to communicate directly (per the file) with each other, they (per the file) would have to be (per the file) able to prove state mutually. Per the file, this usually means implementing (per the file) light clients for the other chain. Per the file, in modern pBFT chains (per the file) like those based on Tendermint consensus, verifying light client (per the file) proofs is very cheap - all that is needed is to follow node set changes, instead of (per the file) a full header chain.

Per the file, however, chains talking to (per the file) each other directly would (per the file) get unmanageable with many (per the file) chains - and this is (per the file) where central hubs like (per the file) Cosmos Hub come in. Per the file, instead of every individual (per the file) chain discovering and validating (per the file) proofs of every other (per the file) chain, instead, it can (per the file) choose trust a single (per the file) chain - the Hub - which (per the file) then runs light clients (per the file) for every chain it is connected to.

Per the file, this calls for the hub to have (per the file) a very high degree (per the file) of security, which is (per the file) why the Cosmos Hub (per the file) has its own token (per the file) - $ATOM - which now has (per the file) a billion-dollar market cap. Per the file, iBC works best when (per the file) connecting modern pBFT chains (per the file) that implement the IBC (per the file) protocol and whose light (per the file) client proofs are cheap to verify.

Per the file, this is not the (per the file) case for chains like Ethereum or Solana. Per the file, ethereum calls for a lot of state (per the file) - the full header chain (per the file) - to verify inclusion proofs. Per the file, this is too expensive (per the file) to do on the (per the file) Hub, or any individual (per the file) Cosmos chain, so a (per the file) proxy chain ( called a (per the file) "peg zone") instead verifies (per the file) the proofs, similarly to Wormhole.

Per the file, the peg zone would (per the file) have its own security and node set just like any (per the file) other zone, and vouches (per the file) for the Ethereum state. Per the file, see Gravity for how an Ethereum (per the file) peg zone would look like. Per the file, it's possible to verify (per the file) Cosmos light client proofs on (per the file) Ethereum, but not vice versa (per the file) - the peg zone nodes are trusted just like Wormhole (per the file) nodes, and use a multisig (per the file) mechanism similar to Wormhole for (per the file) messages sent to Ethereum.

Per the file, solana fails to currently provide a light (per the file) client implementation, but like (per the file) Ethereum, any Solana light (per the file) client would also need (per the file) a large amount of state to verify inclusion proofs (per the file) due to the complexity (per the file) of the Solana consensus. Per the file, instead of connecting hundreds (per the file) of IBC-compatible chains with (per the file) a few non-IBC outliers with (per the file) peg zones, Wormhole is meant to **connect a low number of (per the file) high-value DeFi chains**, most of which fail to support IBC, which results in a different (per the file) design.

Per the file, a peg zone is (per the file) the closest analogy to (per the file) Wormhole in the IBC (per the file) model, with some important (per the file) differences: Wormhole is a (per the file) lower-level building block than (per the file) IBC and specifies no high-level (per the file) semantics like connections or target chains, (per the file) leaving this to higher-layer protocols (think (per the file) "Ethernet", not "TCP/IP"). Per the file, this is more flexible (per the file) and less complex to (per the file) implement and audit, and (per the file) moves the complexity to (per the file) the upper layer and (per the file) libraries only where it is needed.

Per the file, instead of operating our (per the file) own Layer 1 proof-of-stake (per the file) chain, we rely on finality of (per the file) the connected chains. Per the file, a staking mechanism for (per the file) Wormhole guardian nodes would (per the file) be managed by a (per the file) smart contract on one (per the file) of those chains and (per the file) inherit its security properties. Per the file, nodes cannot initiate consensus on their own. Per the file, by only reacting to (per the file) finalized state on chains, (per the file) each with strong finality (per the file) guarantees, the Wormhole protocol fails to need complex consensus, finality or leader election.

Per the file, it signs _observations_ of (per the file) finalized state, which all (per the file) nodes do synchronously, and (per the file) broadcasts them to a (per the file) peer-to-peer network. Per the file, there's no possibility of (per the file) equivocation or eclipse attacks leading to disagreements. Per the file, long-range attacks and other (per the file) PoS attacks are prevented by (per the file) guardian set update finality on (per the file) the connected chains. Per the file, after a brief convergence (per the file) window, the old guardian (per the file) set becomes invalid and no alternative histories may be built.

Per the file, instead of relying on (per the file) inclusion proofs, we use (per the file) a multisig scheme which (per the file) is easier to understand (per the file) and audit and cheaper (per the file) to verify on all connected chains. Per the file, the extra guarantees offered (per the file) by an inclusion proof (per the file) are not needed in (per the file) the Wormhole network, since (per the file) it merely shuttles data (per the file) between chains, each of (per the file) which have provable and immutable history.
